explanation: Keras calls build(input_shape) automatically the first time a layer processes an input, letting you create weights whose shapes depend on the actual input dimensions (e.g., the number of input features), rather than requiring that information to be hardcoded at layer construction time.

q: In a custom PyTorch nn.Module, why is it necessary to call super().__init__() before assigning any submodules/parameters?
options: It's entirely optional and has no functional purpose

nn.Module's __init__ sets up internal bookkeeping (e.g., dictionaries tracking parameters/submodules) that attribute assignment relies on via __setattr__ overrides; skipping it breaks parameter registration
It only affects the string representation printed for the model
It disables GPU support for the module if skipped
explanation: nn.Module's constructor initializes internal dictionaries (like _parameters and _modules) used by its overridden __setattr__ to automatically register any nn.Parameter or nn.Module attributes you assign. Skipping super().__init__() means these registries don't exist, breaking that automatic tracking.

q: What is a key advantage of writing a custom training loop with tf.GradientTape over using model.fit(), for research purposes?
options: model.fit() cannot correctly train any model at all

A custom loop gives explicit, fine-grained control over the forward pass, loss computation, and gradient application, useful for non-standard training procedures (e.g., GANs, custom multi-loss setups) that don't fit the standard fit() API cleanly
GradientTape only works outside of any Keras model
Custom loops eliminate the need for an optimizer entirely
explanation: model.fit() is convenient for standard supervised training but is less flexible for non-standard setups (like alternating generator/discriminator updates in a GAN); a custom tf.GradientTape loop lets you explicitly control exactly what gradients are computed and how they're applied at each step.

q: Why is mask_zero=True commonly used with a Keras Embedding layer when processing padded sequences?
options: It removes padding tokens from the dataset permanently
It propagates a mask so downstream layers (like RNNs) know to ignore the padded timesteps rather than treating them as real input
It forces all embeddings in the layer to be zero
It disables the embedding lookup operation entirely
explanation: Setting mask_zero=True tells the Embedding layer to treat index 0 as padding and generate a mask tensor, which downstream mask-aware layers (like LSTM or GRU) use to skip computation on padded timesteps rather than treating them as meaningful input.

q: What is the benefit of using sinusoidal positional encodings (as in the original Transformer) instead of learned positional embeddings?
options: They require the overall model to be smaller
They can in principle generalize to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training, since they're defined by a fixed mathematical function rather than learned per-position vectors
They eliminate the need for the attention mechanism
They are only usable in RNN-based architectures
explanation: Because sinusoidal encodings are computed from a fixed formula based on position (rather than being learned lookup vectors tied to specific positions seen during training), they can, in theory, be evaluated for positions beyond the maximum sequence length encountered during training.

q: Why do many NLP models tie the weights of the input embedding matrix and the output softmax projection matrix?
options: It's a strict framework requirement with no other rationale
It reduces the number of parameters and can improve performance, since both matrices conceptually map between the same vocabulary/embedding space
Tied weights disable training of the embedding layer entirely
It forces the vocabulary size to be fixed at exactly 1
explanation: Since the input embedding maps token IDs to vectors and the output projection maps vectors back to a distribution over the same vocabulary, sharing (tying) these weight matrices reduces total parameters and has been shown empirically to often improve language modeling performance.

q: What problem does subword tokenization (e.g., Byte-Pair Encoding, WordPiece) address compared to whole-word tokenization?
options: It removes the need for any vocabulary at all
It handles out-of-vocabulary and rare words by breaking them into frequent subword units, keeping vocabulary size manageable while still representing arbitrary words
It is only usable for processing a single specific language
It guarantees every word maps to exactly one single token
explanation: Subword tokenization builds a vocabulary of frequent character sequences, so rare or unseen words can still be represented by combining known subword pieces, avoiding the huge or incomplete vocabularies that whole-word tokenization requires for open-vocabulary text.

q: In relative positional encoding schemes (as used in some Transformer variants), what is encoded instead of absolute token position?
options: Nothing; relative encodings ignore position information entirely
The relative distance/offset between a pair of tokens (query and key), which can generalize better to varying sequence lengths and relative structure
The exact pixel location of a token within an image
The batch index that a token belongs to
explanation: Rather than encoding each token's absolute position in the sequence, relative positional encoding schemes represent the offset/distance between pairs of tokens directly in the attention computation, which can generalize better across different sequence lengths and better capture position-relative patterns.

q: Why is the 'log-sum-exp trick' used when computing log-softmax or cross-entropy loss numerically?
options: It has no actual effect on the numerical computation
Subtracting the maximum logit before exponentiating prevents overflow from large exponentials while producing a mathematically equivalent, numerically stable result
It changes the underlying mathematical result of the softmax function
It is only relevant when working with integer-valued tensors
explanation: Directly exponentiating large logits can overflow floating-point representation. Subtracting the maximum logit before exponentiating bounds the exponent arguments to be at most zero, avoiding overflow, while the algebra guarantees the final normalized result is unchanged.

q: Why do frameworks typically provide a combined 'logits + cross-entropy' loss function rather than requiring users to apply softmax then log then negative log-likelihood manually?
options: There's no real difference; both approaches are equally numerically stable
The combined implementation can internally use numerically stable formulations (like log-sum-exp) and avoid computing intermediate probabilities that could underflow/overflow
Combined loss functions are always computationally slower
Manually computing softmax then log always yields a different mathematical answer
explanation: By fusing softmax and cross-entropy into a single operation working directly on raw logits, the implementation can use numerically stable tricks internally (like log-sum-exp) and avoid materializing potentially tiny or huge intermediate probability values that could lose precision or overflow.

q: What is a common cause of a loss becoming NaN early in training that is unrelated to data corruption?
options: Using too small a batch size, and nothing else
A learning rate that's too high combined with poor initialization or unstable operations (e.g., unclipped exponentials or divisions by near-zero values), causing exploding values
NaN losses are always caused exclusively by hardware failures
NaN losses cannot occur in PyTorch, only in TensorFlow
explanation: An overly aggressive learning rate, combined with numerically fragile operations (like unclipped exponentials in a custom loss, or dividing by a near-zero normalization statistic), can cause weight or activation values to blow up to inf, which quickly propagates to NaN.

q: Why might adding a small epsilon term to a denominator (e.g., in normalization layers or Adam's update) be necessary for numerical stability?
options: It has no real mathematical purpose and is purely stylistic
It prevents division by exactly zero or near-zero variance/second-moment estimates, which would otherwise produce inf or NaN values
It always changes the final trained accuracy by a large, significant margin
It is only relevant when computing with integer tensors
explanation: In operations like BatchNorm (dividing by standard deviation) or Adam's update (dividing by the square root of the second-moment estimate), a variance or moment estimate that's exactly or nearly zero could cause division by zero; adding a small epsilon guards against that instability.

q: Why can computing variance as E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 be less numerically stable than a two-pass or Welford-style algorithm, particularly in float16?
options: There is no numerical stability difference between these approaches at all
Subtracting two large, similar-magnitude quantities can produce significant floating-point cancellation error, especially problematic in lower-precision formats
E[X^2] cannot be computed at all in floating-point arithmetic
This formula only applies to categorical (non-numeric) data
explanation: When E[X^2] and (E[X])^2 are both large and close in value, subtracting them can lead to catastrophic cancellation, amplifying rounding error — this is especially problematic in lower-precision formats like FP16, where Welford's online algorithm or a two-pass computation is more numerically stable.

q: What is a key advantage of Bayesian optimization over grid search for hyperparameter tuning?
options: Bayesian optimization always exhaustively tries every possible combination

Bayesian optimization builds a probabilistic model of the objective function to intelligently select the next promising hyperparameters to try, typically finding good configurations with far fewer trials than exhaustive grid search
Grid search always converges faster in high-dimensional search spaces
Bayesian optimization requires no objective function to evaluate
explanation: Bayesian optimization maintains a surrogate probabilistic model (e.g., a Gaussian process) of how hyperparameters relate to performance, using it to choose the next configuration expected to be most informative or promising, typically requiring far fewer evaluations than exhaustively searching a grid.

q: Why is random search often more efficient than grid search when only a few hyperparameters strongly affect performance?
options: Random search always evaluates fewer configurations than grid search for the same time budget

Random search explores more distinct values along each individual hyperparameter dimension for a given budget, so it's more likely to hit good values of the important hyperparameters than a fixed grid
Grid search cannot handle continuous-valued hyperparameters at all
Random search is guaranteed to always find the global optimum
explanation: In a grid search, many trials waste budget varying unimportant hyperparameters at fixed important-hyperparameter values. Random search, by sampling independently, covers a wider range of values along each important dimension for the same total number of trials, increasing the chance of finding a good setting.

q: What does the 'Hyperband' algorithm do to speed up hyperparameter search compared to fully training every configuration?
options: It trains every configuration for the maximum number of epochs regardless of early performance
It allocates a small training budget to many configurations first, then progressively eliminates poor performers and allocates more budget to promising ones (successive halving)
It only ever searches over the learning rate, ignoring other hyperparameters
It requires no validation data of any kind to operate
explanation: Hyperband combines random sampling of configurations with a successive-halving strategy: it starts many configurations with a small budget (e.g., few epochs), then keeps only the best-performing subset and gives them progressively larger budgets, efficiently allocating compute toward promising candidates.

q: Why is it important to re-tune hyperparameters like learning rate when significantly increasing batch size?
options: Batch size has no meaningful effect on the optimal learning rate

Larger batches produce lower-variance gradient estimates, which often permits (or, for similar convergence behavior, requires) scaling the learning rate up, following heuristics like the linear scaling rule
Increasing batch size always requires proportionally decreasing the learning rate
Batch size can only ever be changed together with the number of network layers
explanation: Because larger batches average over more examples, gradient estimates become less noisy, and empirically a proportionally larger learning rate (as in the linear scaling rule) is often needed to maintain similar training dynamics and convergence speed as with the original smaller batch size.

q: Why can hyperparameter tuning based only on a single train/validation split be misleading, motivating the use of cross-validation or repeated runs?
options: A single split always gives the exact same result as any other split would
A single split's validation performance is subject to noise/variance from that particular data partition and random initialization, so it may not reliably reflect true generalization performance
Cross-validation removes the need for a separate test set entirely
Single train/validation splits are only ever used for classification tasks
explanation: A single validation split's measured performance depends on which specific examples ended up in that split as well as random initialization/training noise; averaging over multiple splits (cross-validation) or repeated runs gives a more robust, less noise-sensitive estimate of true generalization performance.

q: What is the core limitation of greedy decoding in sequence generation that beam search aims to address?
options: Greedy decoding is prohibitively too slow for any practical use

Greedy decoding commits to the single highest-probability token at each step, which can lead to a globally suboptimal full sequence; beam search keeps multiple candidate hypotheses to explore a larger portion of the search space
Greedy decoding cannot be used together with RNN-based decoders
Greedy decoding always produces the mathematically optimal full sequence
explanation: Because greedy decoding locks in the locally best token at each step without considering how that choice affects future steps, it can miss a higher-probability overall sequence; beam search keeps several top candidate partial sequences alive at each step, exploring more of the space before committing.

q: What is the role of the attention mechanism in a classic encoder-decoder seq2seq model (e.g., Bahdanau attention)?
options: It replaces the encoder network entirely

It lets the decoder, at each output step, compute a weighted combination over all encoder hidden states, focusing on the most relevant parts of the input rather than relying solely on a single fixed-length context vector
It removes the need for a decoder RNN altogether
It only operates during training and is disabled at inference time
explanation: Instead of compressing the entire input into one fixed-size vector, attention computes, at each decoding step, a weighted sum over all encoder hidden states based on relevance to the current decoding step, letting the decoder dynamically focus on different parts of the input as needed.

q: Why does using only the final encoder hidden state as context (in early seq2seq models without attention) become a bottleneck for long input sequences?
options: It has no negative effect regardless of how long the input sequence is
A single fixed-size vector must compress all information from an arbitrarily long input sequence, causing information loss that worsens as sequence length grows
It causes the decoder to completely ignore the input sequence
It only ever affects very short input sequences, not long ones
explanation: Squeezing an entire, potentially long input sequence into one fixed-dimensional vector inevitably loses information as sequence length increases, making it harder for the decoder to recover fine-grained details needed to generate an accurate output — a bottleneck attention was designed to relieve.

q: What does 'length normalization' address when using beam search to compare hypotheses of different lengths?
options: It has no real purpose and is essentially never used in practice

Without it, cumulative log-probability naturally favors shorter sequences (since each additional token multiplies in a probability <= 1), so length normalization divides/adjusts scores to fairly compare hypotheses of different lengths
It forces all generated sequences to be exactly the same length
It only applies specifically to image captioning models
explanation: Because summing log-probabilities over more tokens tends to produce a more negative (lower) total score, naive beam search comparisons would systematically favor shorter outputs; length normalization (e.g., dividing by sequence length, possibly with a penalty exponent) corrects for this bias when ranking candidate hypotheses.

q: In scheduled sampling, how does the probability of using the model's own prediction (versus the ground truth) as the next decoder input typically change over training?
options: It stays fixed at 0% for the entire duration of training
It's typically annealed to gradually increase over training, moving from mostly teacher forcing early on to more reliance on the model's own predictions later, easing the train/inference mismatch
It's always set to 100% starting from the very first training step
It only ever applies to convolutional models, never RNNs
explanation: Scheduled sampling starts training with mostly ground-truth inputs (teacher forcing) for stability, then gradually increases the probability of instead feeding the model's own predicted tokens as training progresses, helping bridge the gap between training and the fully autoregressive inference procedure.

q: What is the purpose of the ModelCheckpoint callback's save_best_only=True option in Keras?
options: It saves a checkpoint at every single training batch regardless of performance
It only overwrites the saved checkpoint file when the monitored metric improves, avoiding storage of worse-performing intermediate models
It disables checkpoint saving entirely for the whole run
It saves only the optimizer's internal state, never the model weights
explanation: With save_best_only=True, ModelCheckpoint compares each epoch's monitored metric to the best seen so far and only writes a new checkpoint file when there's an improvement, so the saved file always reflects the best-performing model seen during training.

q: What does the Keras EarlyStopping callback's restore_best_weights=True option do?
options: Nothing different from the callback's default behavior
When training stops, it reloads the model's weights from the epoch with the best monitored metric value rather than leaving the weights from the final (possibly worse) epoch
It restores the model to its original, randomly initialized state
It restores the training dataset to its original unshuffled order
explanation: Without this option, when EarlyStopping halts training, the model is left with whatever weights it had at the final (post-patience) epoch, which may already be overfit. restore_best_weights=True reverts the model to the weights that achieved the best monitored metric value during training.

q: How does the Keras ReduceLROnPlateau callback decide when to reduce the learning rate?
options: It reduces the learning rate at fixed, predetermined epoch numbers regardless of performance
It monitors a specified metric (e.g., validation loss) and reduces the learning rate by a factor when that metric stops improving for a specified number of epochs ('patience')
It increases the learning rate whenever the training loss decreases
It has no relationship to any monitored metric whatsoever
explanation: ReduceLROnPlateau watches a chosen metric each epoch, and if it fails to improve for a set number of consecutive epochs (the patience), the callback multiplies the current learning rate by a specified reduction factor, hoping smaller steps help escape the plateau.

q: What is the primary use of TensorBoard's histogram/distribution tab during model debugging?
options: It shows only the single final test accuracy number
It visualizes how weight, bias, and activation/gradient distributions evolve across training steps, helping diagnose issues like vanishing gradients or dead units
It only displays the dataset's raw input images
It replaces the need for a validation set entirely
explanation: The histogram tab plots how the distributions of weights, biases, activations, and gradients change over training steps, which can reveal issues like gradients shrinking toward zero (vanishing gradients) or a growing fraction of dead ReLU units.

q: Why might you implement a custom Keras callback (subclassing tf.keras.callbacks.Callback) rather than using built-in callbacks?
options: Custom callbacks are strictly required for every Keras model to function at all

To hook custom logic (e.g., custom logging, dynamic hyperparameter changes, custom early-stopping criteria) into specific points of the training loop, like on_epoch_end or on_batch_end, that built-in callbacks don't cover
Custom callbacks permanently disable the optimizer
Built-in callbacks cannot be combined together with each other
explanation: Subclassing Callback lets you override hook methods like on_epoch_end, on_batch_begin, etc., to inject arbitrary custom behavior into the training loop at precise points, useful whenever the built-in callbacks (checkpointing, early stopping, LR reduction) don't cover a project's specific needs.

q: What is the purpose of a forward hook registered via register_forward_hook on a PyTorch module?
options: It permanently changes the module's learned weights
It lets you run custom code (e.g., inspecting or modifying intermediate activations) automatically every time that module's forward pass executes, without altering its source code
It only works during the backward pass, not the forward pass
It replaces the model's loss function
explanation: A forward hook is a callback function that PyTorch automatically invokes right after a module's forward() method runs, letting you inspect or even modify the module's output on the fly — useful for debugging, feature extraction, or activation analysis without editing the model's code.

q: Why might you configure different parameter groups with different learning rates in a PyTorch optimizer (e.g., torch.optim.Adam([{...}, {...}]))?
options: PyTorch optimizers only ever support a single global learning rate with no exceptions
To apply different learning rates (or other hyperparameters like weight decay) to different parts of the model, such as a lower rate for a pretrained backbone and a higher rate for a newly added head
Parameter groups are purely cosmetic and don't actually affect training
It is a mandatory requirement for every PyTorch model regardless of use case
explanation: Passing a list of parameter-group dictionaries to a PyTorch optimizer lets you assign distinct hyperparameters (like learning rate) to different subsets of parameters, a common technique in transfer learning where a pretrained backbone often uses a smaller learning rate than a freshly initialized head.

q: What does torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint do, and what tradeoff does it introduce?
options: It saves the entire model to disk periodically during training
It avoids storing intermediate activations for a wrapped segment of the network during the forward pass, recomputing them during backward, trading extra compute time for reduced memory usage
It disables gradient computation entirely for the wrapped segment
It converts the wrapped segment of the network to run only on the CPU
explanation: Checkpointing a segment of the network means its intermediate activations aren't kept in memory after the forward pass; instead, they're recomputed by re-running the forward pass for that segment during backpropagation, reducing peak memory usage at the cost of extra forward computation.

q: What does torch.vmap (or functorch's vmap) let you do that is otherwise awkward to express efficiently?
options: It permanently changes a function to operate in-place on its inputs

It automatically vectorizes a function written for a single example so it can be applied efficiently across a batch dimension without manually writing a Python loop, often mapping to efficient batched operations
It replaces the need for a GPU device entirely
It disables autograd tracking for the vectorized function
explanation: vmap takes a function defined to operate on a single example and automatically transforms it into a batched version that applies across an added batch dimension, avoiding slow explicit Python loops while typically mapping to efficient vectorized/batched tensor operations under the hood.

q: Why does calling .item() on a GPU tensor inside a tight training loop (e.g., to log loss every step) potentially hurt performance?
options: .item() has no performance cost whatsoever in any context

.item() forces a synchronization between the CPU and GPU (waiting for all queued GPU work to finish) to transfer the scalar value back to Python, which can stall the otherwise asynchronous GPU pipeline if done too frequently
.item() only works on CPU tensors, so it always throws an error on GPU tensors
.item() automatically moves the entire model to the CPU device
explanation: GPU operations are typically queued and executed asynchronously relative to the CPU. Calling .item() requires the actual scalar value, forcing the CPU to wait for all pending GPU operations to complete before it can read that value back, which — if done every iteration — can repeatedly stall the pipeline and hurt throughput.

q: What is the main purpose of tf.data.Dataset.cache()?
options: It permanently shuffles the dataset once and for all
It stores the elements produced by the dataset (in memory or to a file) after the first pass so subsequent epochs can reuse them without re-executing upstream reading/preprocessing
It automatically splits the dataset across all available GPUs
It converts the dataset into a NumPy array
explanation: cache() saves the output of the pipeline up to that point the first time it's iterated, so later epochs can replay those cached elements instead of redoing expensive I/O or preprocessing, at the cost of memory or disk space.

q: Why is passing tf.data.AUTOTUNE as num_parallel_calls to Dataset.map() often preferred over a fixed integer?
options: It disables parallelism entirely for safety
It lets tf.data dynamically tune the level of parallelism at runtime based on available CPU resources and pipeline behavior, instead of requiring the user to hand-pick a value
It forces the map function to run on the GPU only
It guarantees deterministic ordering regardless of other settings
explanation: AUTOTUNE hands the parallelism decision to tf.data's runtime, which observes resource usage and pipeline throughput and adjusts the number of parallel calls automatically, often outperforming a manually chosen fixed value.

q: What is the primary use case for tf.data.Dataset.interleave()?
options: To compute the elementwise sum of two datasets
To concurrently interleave elements read from multiple source datasets (e.g., many files), improving I/O parallelism instead of processing sources strictly one after another
To permanently sort dataset elements by label
To convert a dataset into a Keras Sequential model
explanation: interleave() applies a function that maps each input element to a dataset, then interleaves elements across the resulting datasets, commonly used to read from many files concurrently rather than exhausting one file before opening the next.

q: What is a key limitation of tf.data.Dataset.from_generator() compared to a TFRecord-based pipeline?
options: It cannot be used with model.fit() under any circumstances

Because it wraps an arbitrary Python generator, it runs under the Python GIL and typically can't parallelize or serialize as efficiently as native tf.data source ops reading serialized formats like TFRecord
It requires the entire dataset to already be a dense NumPy array
It only supports scalar (rank-0) outputs
explanation: from_generator() executes Python code to produce elements, which is bound by the GIL and harder for tf.data to parallelize/prefetch as efficiently as reading pre-serialized binary formats, making it a common performance bottleneck for large pipelines.

q: What does setting a tf.data.Options object's deterministic field to False allow?
options: It permanently disables batching

It lets parallel transformations like map/interleave produce elements out of their original order in exchange for potentially higher throughput, since the pipeline no longer has to wait to emit results in strict sequence
It forces every dataset element to be reprocessed twice
It converts the dataset to run only on TPU
explanation: When determinism isn't required, allowing out-of-order results from parallel map/interleave lets tf.data return whichever parallel worker finishes first rather than blocking on strict input order, which can meaningfully improve throughput.

q: What is the purpose of tf.data.Dataset.shard(num_shards, index) in a distributed training setup?
options: It duplicates the full dataset identically on every worker
It gives each worker a distinct, non-overlapping subset of the dataset based on its index, so multiple workers can each process a different portion of the data without redundant work
It randomly deletes a fraction of the dataset permanently
It merges multiple datasets into a single shared file
explanation: shard() partitions a dataset into num_shards disjoint pieces and returns only the piece at the given index, which is how independent workers in a distributed job can each consume a different, non-overlapping slice of the data.

q: Why is the TFRecord format commonly used for large-scale tf.data training pipelines instead of many individual small files?
options: TFRecord files cannot be read in parallel at all

TFRecord stores data as a sequence of binary serialized records optimized for fast, largely sequential reads, which better matches tf.data's I/O and prefetching model than opening huge numbers of small individual files
TFRecord automatically performs data augmentation on read
TFRecord is required before any model can call model.fit()
explanation: Sequential binary reads of a smaller number of larger TFRecord files are typically far more I/O-efficient than opening and reading enormous numbers of tiny individual files, especially on networked or spinning-disk storage.

q: Why might you set drop_remainder=True when calling Dataset.batch() for TPU training?
options: To increase the total size of the dataset
To guarantee every batch has an identical, statically known size, which TPU/XLA compilation generally requires since a smaller final partial batch would introduce a different, dynamically-sized shape
To disable shuffling for the rest of training
To force the dataset to repeat indefinitely
explanation: TPUs (via XLA) compile ahead of time for fixed shapes; an irregular final batch smaller than the rest would trigger a different shape and costly recompilation (or an outright error), so dropping it keeps every batch uniformly sized.

q: What memory advantage does passing a tf.data.Dataset (instead of full in-memory NumPy arrays) to model.fit() typically provide for very large datasets?
options: It has no advantage; both approaches use identical memory
It streams and processes data batch by batch on demand rather than requiring the entire dataset to be loaded into memory at once, which scales to datasets far larger than available RAM
It automatically compresses the trained model's weights
It removes the need for any batching or shuffling logic
explanation: A tf.data pipeline reads, transforms, and yields only the data needed for the current (and soon-to-be-prefetched) batches, whereas loading full NumPy arrays into memory upfront requires the whole dataset to fit in RAM.

q: When calling Dataset.repeat() with no arguments and training with model.fit(steps_per_epoch=N), what defines the boundary of an 'epoch'?
options: TensorFlow automatically detects the true end of the underlying data
repeat() makes the dataset repeat indefinitely, so steps_per_epoch is what explicitly defines how many batches constitute one epoch, rather than the dataset's own natural end being used
The dataset stops after exactly one epoch regardless of repeat()
steps_per_epoch is ignored whenever repeat() is used
explanation: Without a fixed size, an infinitely repeating dataset has no natural 'end of epoch,' so steps_per_epoch tells fit() exactly how many batches to draw before considering an epoch complete and firing epoch-level callbacks.

q: What is the purpose of Dataset.prefetch(buffer_size=tf.data.AUTOTUNE) at the end of a tf.data pipeline?
options: It permanently caches the dataset to disk

It overlaps preparation of upcoming batches (on the CPU) with the consumption of the current batch (e.g., GPU/TPU compute), reducing accelerator idle time, with AUTOTUNE letting the runtime pick the buffer size
It reverses the order of all elements in the dataset
It forces synchronous, single-threaded execution
explanation: prefetch() decouples producing the next batches from consuming the current one, so the CPU can be readying future batches while the accelerator is busy computing on the current one, and AUTOTUNE lets tf.data tune the buffer size dynamically.

q: What is the primary use case for Dataset.window() combined with flat_map() in a tf.data pipeline?
options: To permanently discard every other element of the dataset

To construct fixed-size sliding windows over a sequential dataset (e.g., for time-series or language-model training), which the resulting nested dataset-of-datasets is then flattened back into batched tensors
To convert a dataset into a scalar constant
To disable prefetching for the remainder of the pipeline
explanation: window() groups consecutive elements into sub-datasets representing sliding or tumbling windows, and flat_map() (often paired with .batch() on each window) flattens these back into a usable dataset of fixed-length sequence examples.

q: What does Dataset.cache(filename) do differently from Dataset.cache() with no argument?
options: It disables caching entirely
It writes the cached elements to disk at the given file path rather than keeping them only in memory, letting the cache persist beyond a single process and handle datasets too large to fit in RAM
It caches only the dataset's labels, never the features
It forces the dataset to re-download from the internet each time
explanation: Providing a filename tells cache() to persist the materialized elements to disk-backed files instead of an in-memory cache, which is useful when the dataset is too large to comfortably fit in memory but reprocessing it repeatedly is still expensive.

q: When using Dataset.interleave() or .map() with parallel calls and non-deterministic ordering enabled, what tradeoff is being made?
options: Accuracy is permanently reduced in exchange for smaller model size
Elements may be emitted out of their original order in exchange for higher achievable throughput, since the pipeline no longer waits to preserve strict sequential ordering across parallel workers
The dataset becomes read-only and can never be iterated again
Labels and features become permanently disconnected from each other
explanation: Enforcing strict in-order output can force the pipeline to wait for a specific slow parallel worker to finish before yielding an already-completed later element; relaxing that requirement lets faster workers' results flow through immediately, improving throughput.

q: What is the purpose of TensorBoard's 'Input Pipeline Analyzer' (via the TF Profiler)?
options: It visualizes the model's final classification accuracy only
It helps diagnose whether training is input-bound by showing how much time is spent waiting on the tf.data pipeline versus actual device (GPU/TPU) computation, guiding where to optimize
It automatically rewrites the model architecture for better accuracy
It permanently disables the tf.data pipeline being profiled
explanation: The Input Pipeline Analyzer breaks down step time into data-loading/preprocessing versus device compute, making it clear whether the accelerator is frequently starved waiting on tf.data (an input bottleneck) versus being the actual bottleneck itself.

q: What does it mean for a tf.function-decorated Python function to be 'polymorphic'?
options: It can only ever be called with exactly one fixed input signature

A single tf.function object can dispatch to multiple underlying traced graphs (ConcreteFunctions), one per distinct combination of input shapes/dtypes (and non-tensor argument values) it has been called with
It automatically converts itself into a Keras model
It disables gradient computation for every call
explanation: The high-level tf.function wrapper is polymorphic: it transparently traces and caches a separate ConcreteFunction for each unique input signature it encounters, dispatching future calls to the matching already-traced graph when possible.

q: What does calling tf.autograph.to_code() on a Python function let you inspect?
options: The compiled machine code that will run on the GPU

The generated Python source code that results from AutoGraph's transformation of the original function (e.g., converting Python control flow into TensorFlow graph ops), useful for debugging conversion issues
The exact runtime in milliseconds of the traced function
The list of GPUs currently visible to TensorFlow
explanation: to_code() renders the intermediate, AutoGraph-rewritten Python source (with control-flow constructs replaced by their tf.autograph-compatible equivalents), which is a useful debugging tool when a tf.function isn't behaving as expected.

q: Why do Python side effects inside a tf.function-decorated function (e.g., appending to a Python list, incrementing a plain Python counter) typically only happen once rather than on every call?
options: Such side effects are automatically re-run identically on every single call

Because tracing executes the Python code once to build the graph, and any pure-Python statements not corresponding to TensorFlow ops are baked into that one trace rather than being re-executed on subsequent (graph-mode) calls
tf.function permanently disables all Python code inside it
Python side effects are converted into TensorFlow variables automatically
explanation: Only TensorFlow ops get captured into the traced graph and re-executed on each call; ordinary Python-level side effects run just once, during the tracing pass, so relying on them to happen every call is a common source of bugs.

q: What is the purpose of reducing retracing (e.g., via reduce_retracing or by relaxing shapes) for a tf.function?
options: To force a new trace on every single call for maximum safety

To let TensorFlow generalize a traced graph across a range of similar input shapes (e.g., by treating a varying dimension as unknown), avoiding the overhead of creating and caching a brand-new trace for every slightly different shape encountered
To permanently disable GPU execution for the function
To convert the function into eager mode only
explanation: Frequent retracing (one trace per distinct shape) is costly; allowing the traced graph to use a more general (partially unknown) shape signature lets a single trace handle many actual input shapes, cutting down on repeated compilation overhead.

q: What is a tf.function's ConcreteFunction?
options: A Keras layer with no trainable parameters
A single specific traced graph produced for one particular input signature, as opposed to the outer polymorphic tf.function object which can hold and dispatch among many such traces
The eager-mode Python function before any tracing occurs
A checkpoint file storing only optimizer state
explanation: While the decorated tf.function is a polymorphic wrapper that can trace multiple graphs, each individual trace for one exact input signature is captured as a ConcreteFunction, which can itself be extracted, inspected, or exported.

q: Why does calling a tf.function-decorated function that creates a new tf.Variable inside it sometimes raise an error on later calls?
options: TensorFlow forbids the use of tf.Variable anywhere inside a tf.function

Variables are generally expected to be created only once (e.g., on the first call); TensorFlow disallows creating new variables during a retrace of an already-traced function to avoid silently duplicating or re-initializing state
tf.Variable objects cannot ever be used with GPUs
Every call to a tf.function must create identical new variables by design
explanation: Repeatedly creating a variable inside a function meant to be called many times would either duplicate state or need special handling every call; TF enforces that variable creation typically happens once, raising an error if it detects variable creation happening again on a later trace/call.

q: What is the purpose of tf.py_function?
options: To permanently convert a whole model into TFLite format

To let you execute arbitrary Python code, including non-TensorFlow operations, inside an otherwise graph-based computation, at the cost of reduced compatibility with things like XLA compilation, distribution strategies, and graph serialization
To disable eager execution globally for the entire program
To automatically parallelize any Python function across all GPUs
explanation: tf.py_function wraps a Python function so it can be called from within a graph, useful for logic that can't be expressed as TF ops, but the wrapped code runs as opaque Python, which limits portability, serialization, and optimizations like XLA.

q: Why can wrapping many very small operations each in their own separate @tf.function sometimes hurt performance rather than help it?
options: @tf.function always makes every program strictly slower with no exceptions

Each Python-to-graph call boundary carries overhead, and splitting logic into many small traced functions can prevent TensorFlow from fusing/optimizing operations across those boundaries, whereas wrapping a larger coherent chunk of computation in one tf.function allows more effective optimization
Small tf.function calls automatically disable the GPU
It causes gradients to be computed twice for every operation
explanation: Excessive function-call boundaries add dispatch overhead and limit the scope over which graph-level optimizations (like op fusion) can operate; consolidating a larger logical unit of work into a single tf.function usually captures more of these benefits.

q: What is the purpose of tf.autograph.experimental.do_not_convert?
options: To force AutoGraph to convert a function twice for safety

To exclude a specific function from AutoGraph's automatic conversion, so it executes as ordinary Python when called from within a tf.function, useful when that function only performs Python-side logic incompatible with graph conversion
To permanently disable gradient tracking for the whole program
To convert a function into a Keras Sequential model
explanation: Marking a function with do_not_convert tells AutoGraph to leave it alone rather than attempting to rewrite its control flow into graph ops, which is useful for helper functions that are pure Python utilities not meant to be traced as graph logic.

q: Why can a tf.function traced with variables created inside a particular tf.distribute.Strategy's scope behave unexpectedly if invoked outside that same distributed context?
options: tf.function objects can never be called more than once regardless of scope

Variables created within a strategy's scope become distributed/mirrored variables tied to specific device placement and synchronization behavior defined by that strategy, so using the resulting function outside that context can produce placement errors or bypass intended synchronization
Strategy scopes have no effect on variable creation whatsoever
It always silently converts the mirrored variables into plain Python lists
explanation: Because tf.distribute strategies control how and where variables are created and replicated, a graph built around variables from one strategy's scope generally assumes that same distributed context for correct behavior, and using it elsewhere can violate those assumptions.

q: Under what condition does AutoGraph convert a Python for loop into a tf.while_loop rather than simply unrolling it at trace time?
options: Whenever the loop body contains more than one statement

When the loop iterates over a tensor whose length isn't known until runtime (e.g., a value from tf.range() computed dynamically), so AutoGraph must generate a dynamic graph loop instead of statically unrolling a fixed number of iterations
AutoGraph never converts Python for loops under any circumstance
Only when the loop explicitly calls tf.while_loop by name
explanation: A for loop over a plain Python list/range with a fixed, statically known length is simply unrolled during tracing, but iterating over a tensor whose size is only known at runtime forces AutoGraph to emit an actual dynamic tf.while_loop graph op.

q: Why does calling .numpy() on a tensor inside a tf.function-traced function typically raise an error?
options: .numpy() is not a real method available on any TensorFlow tensor

During tracing, tensors are symbolic placeholders representing values that will exist only when the graph actually runs, so there's no concrete value yet available for .numpy() to convert, unlike in eager execution where tensors hold real values immediately
.numpy() only works on tensors stored on a TPU
It always succeeds but silently returns zeros
explanation: Inside a traced graph, computations are described symbolically rather than executed immediately, so operations requiring a concrete, already-computed value (like extracting it as a NumPy array) generally aren't available until the graph is actually run.

q: What does passing jit_compile=True to @tf.function do?
options: It disables the function's ability to compute gradients

It forces that specific function to be compiled with XLA, fusing eligible operations into optimized kernels for potential speedups, but requiring the operations involved to be XLA-compatible (often needing largely static shapes)
It automatically converts the function's output into a SavedModel
It makes the function silently run on CPU only, ignoring any GPU
explanation: jit_compile=True is a stricter request than opportunistic global JIT: it mandates XLA compilation for that function, which can yield significant fused-kernel speedups but fails outright if the function contains ops or dynamic shapes XLA can't support.

q: Why can passing a mutable, non-tensor Python default argument to a tf.function lead to confusing caching/behavior across calls?
options: Non-tensor Python arguments are always ignored completely by tf.function

Non-tensor argument values become part of what distinguishes one traced signature from another, so a function relying on a mutable default (a classic Python pitfall evaluated once) combined with tf.function's per-signature trace caching can produce stale or unexpectedly reused behavior across calls
tf.function forces every default argument to become a required argument
Mutable defaults automatically convert into tf.Variable objects
explanation: Because tf.function treats distinct Python (non-tensor) argument values as distinct signatures worth a separate trace, combining that with Python's well-known mutable-default-argument gotcha can produce surprising results where a stale, shared mutable object is reused across calls.

q: What does tf.distribute.MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy add on top of a single-machine MirroredStrategy?
options: It removes the need for synchronized gradient updates entirely

It extends synchronous, mirrored data-parallel training across multiple separate machines (each potentially with several GPUs), coordinating gradient synchronization across machines rather than only across devices on one host
It only supports training on a single CPU core
It converts the model to run exclusively on TPUs
explanation: MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy generalizes MirroredStrategy's synchronous, all-reduce-based training beyond one machine's devices to multiple worker machines, each contributing their own GPUs, while still keeping training synchronous across the whole cluster.

q: What is the purpose of the TF_CONFIG environment variable in multi-worker TensorFlow training?
options: It sets the batch size used for every training step

It specifies the cluster configuration (the list of worker/chief/parameter-server addresses) and identifies the current process's own task type and index, so each process knows its role and how to reach the others
It controls only the logging verbosity level
It stores the trained model's final weights
explanation: TF_CONFIG is a JSON-formatted environment variable that each process in a distributed job reads to learn the full cluster topology and its own place within it (e.g., 'worker' index 2), which distribution strategies rely on to coordinate correctly.

q: How does tf.distribute.ParameterServerStrategy's architecture generally differ from a synchronous strategy like MirroredStrategy?
options: It requires every device to hold an identical, fully mirrored copy of every variable at all times

Variables are held on separate parameter-server tasks while worker tasks compute gradients and push updates, commonly in an asynchronous fashion, rather than every replica synchronously all-reducing gradients each step
It can only ever run on a single machine with a single GPU
It disables the use of any optimizer during training
explanation: In the parameter-server pattern, model variables live centrally on dedicated parameter-server tasks; worker tasks compute gradients against a copy of the variables and send updates back, which can happen asynchronously, contrasting with fully synchronous, mirrored all-reduce training.

q: In multi-worker distributed training, what additional responsibilities does the 'chief' worker typically have compared to other workers?
options: The chief performs no computation at all and only observes

The chief usually additionally handles tasks like writing checkpoints, saving the final model, and logging summaries, so these actions happen exactly once rather than being redundantly duplicated by every worker
Only the chief is allowed to compute gradients
The chief always uses a completely different model architecture from the other workers
explanation: While all workers (including the chief) typically perform the same training computation, the chief is designated to additionally perform singleton duties like checkpointing and saving the model, avoiding wasteful or conflicting duplicate writes from every worker.

q: What must typically happen before using tf.distribute.TPUStrategy to run computations on Cloud TPUs?
options: Nothing; TPUStrategy requires no setup beyond importing TensorFlow

A TPUClusterResolver must locate the TPU, and the TPU system must be explicitly initialized (e.g., via tf.tpu.experimental.initialize_tpu_system) before the strategy can be used to place and run computations on the TPU devices
The dataset must first be fully converted into a SparseTensor
The model must be re-implemented using only NumPy operations
explanation: Connecting to and initializing the TPU runtime is a required setup step (resolving the TPU's network address and resetting/initializing its devices) that must occur before TPUStrategy can successfully distribute computation onto the TPU cores.

q: Under a distribution strategy with N replicas in sync, how does the global batch size relate to the per-replica batch size?
options: They are always required to be exactly equal to each other
The global batch size equals the per-replica batch size multiplied by the number of replicas in sync, since each replica processes its own share of a single, larger effective batch every step
The global batch size is always fixed at exactly 1 regardless of replica count
Per-replica batch size has no relationship to the number of replicas
explanation: Because each replica independently processes its own slice of data each step before gradients are synchronized, the effective (global) batch size seen collectively by one training step is the per-replica batch size times the number of synchronized replicas.

q: Why is model creation and compilation typically wrapped inside strategy.scope() when using a tf.distribute strategy with Keras?
options: It has no real effect and is purely a style convention

It ensures the model's variables are created as properly distributed/mirrored variables from the start, matching the strategy's intended replication and synchronization behavior, rather than as ordinary single-device variables
It forces the model to be saved in TFLite format automatically
It disables the optimizer's ability to update weights
explanation: Creating variables inside strategy.scope() lets the strategy control how those variables are instantiated (e.g., mirrored identically across devices), which is necessary for the strategy's synchronization and update logic to work correctly; creating them outside can bypass that setup.

q: In a custom distributed training loop, what does strategy.run(step_fn, args=...) do?
options: It runs step_fn exactly once on a single arbitrary device
It invokes the given step function replicated across each device/replica managed by the strategy, each operating on its own local portion of the data in parallel
It permanently disables gradient computation for step_fn
It converts step_fn into a TFLite-compatible function
explanation: strategy.run() is the mechanism for executing a per-replica computation: it dispatches step_fn to run on every replica the strategy manages, each replica working on its own local slice of the current global batch.

q: What does strategy.reduce() do in a custom distributed training loop?
options: It deletes some of the replicas to save memory
It aggregates per-replica values (such as PerReplica loss values returned from strategy.run) across all replicas into a single combined value, using a specified reduction like SUM or MEAN
It reduces the model's total number of trainable parameters
It disables all further training after being called once
explanation: Since strategy.run() typically returns per-replica values (one per device), strategy.reduce() combines those distributed values into a single aggregated result (e.g., summing or averaging losses across replicas) usable for logging or further computation.

q: In a custom distributed training loop, why is it common to compute per-example loss with Reduction.NONE and then scale it using something like tf.nn.compute_average_loss (dividing by the global batch size) rather than simply averaging each replica's local batch independently?
options: Because global batch size has no effect on gradient correctness

If each replica independently divided by only its own local batch size, then summing the resulting gradients across replicas during all-reduce would effectively over-scale the update relative to a true single global-batch average, so dividing by the global batch size instead keeps the aggregated gradient correctly scaled
Because Reduction.NONE automatically performs the averaging internally with no further code needed
Because compute_average_loss disables gradient computation entirely
explanation: Each replica only sees a fraction of the global batch; if it normalized loss purely by its own local count and gradients from all replicas are then summed via all-reduce, the effective gradient would be scaled incorrectly relative to what a true single-device global-batch computation would produce, so dividing consistently by the global batch size corrects for this.

q: What communication mechanism underlies tf.distribute.MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy's gradient synchronization by default?
options: Gradients are written to a shared spreadsheet file for manual aggregation
It uses TensorFlow's collective communication ops (e.g., ring or hierarchical all-reduce, using NCCL where available) to efficiently synchronize gradients across all GPUs and workers in the cluster
It relies exclusively on emailing weight updates between machines
Synchronization never happens; each worker trains a fully independent model
explanation: Under the hood, MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy is backed by TensorFlow's collective ops implementation, which efficiently all-reduces gradients across all participating devices/workers (leveraging optimized communication libraries like NCCL where the hardware supports it).

q: What is tf.distribute.OneDeviceStrategy primarily used for?
options: Scaling training seamlessly across an entire TPU pod
Testing and validating distribution-strategy-aware code on a single specified device before actually scaling out to multiple devices, without incurring real multi-device distribution overhead
Permanently disabling GPU acceleration
Running multiple entirely separate models simultaneously on different clusters
explanation: OneDeviceStrategy applies the tf.distribute API's structure (scope, variable creation conventions, etc.) while actually running on just one device, which is handy for debugging or validating strategy-compatible code before deploying it on real multi-device/multi-worker hardware.

q: How does tf.distribute.experimental.CentralStorageStrategy differ from MirroredStrategy?
options: They are functionally identical in every respect

CentralStorageStrategy keeps a single copy of variables centrally (e.g., on the CPU) and updates them there, while computation is still mirrored/parallelized across available GPUs, rather than fully replicating variables on every device as MirroredStrategy does
CentralStorageStrategy can only be used with exactly one GPU
MirroredStrategy never synchronizes gradients across devices
explanation: Instead of each GPU holding its own full replica of every variable (as in MirroredStrategy), CentralStorageStrategy centralizes variable storage and updates in one place while still distributing the forward/backward computation across the available GPUs.

q: Why is a dataset typically passed through strategy.experimental_distribute_dataset() (or an equivalent distribution-aware method) rather than used as a plain tf.data.Dataset in a custom distributed training loop?
options: Because plain datasets cannot be iterated over at all

It shards and prepares the dataset so that each replica automatically receives its own correctly-sized portion of every global batch, and wraps the dataset so it plugs correctly into strategy.run()-based iteration
Because it permanently converts the dataset into a SparseTensor
Because it disables shuffling for correctness reasons
explanation: The distribution-aware dataset wrapping ensures that when strategy.run() executes a step across replicas, each replica correctly receives its own slice of the current global batch, handling sharding/distribution details that a plain, un-wrapped dataset wouldn't manage automatically.

q: Why does the scaling efficiency of synchronous multi-worker training often degrade as more workers/machines are added, even though the computational work is parallelized?
options: TensorFlow refuses to run on more than four machines simultaneously

The network bandwidth and latency required for all-reduce gradient synchronization across many machines can become the bottleneck relative to per-worker compute time, especially for large models with many parameters, limiting the benefit of adding further workers
Adding more workers always reduces the effective global batch size
Every additional worker permanently halts training
explanation: As more workers are added, each synchronous step's gradient all-reduce must move increasingly more data (or coordinate more participants) across the network; if that communication cost grows faster than the corresponding reduction in per-worker compute time, overall scaling efficiency suffers.

q: What is a key advantage of the Keras Functional API over the Sequential API?
options: It only allows a single linear stack of layers with one input and one output
It can express arbitrary directed-acyclic-graph architectures with multiple inputs, multiple outputs, and shared/reused layers, which a simple linear Sequential stack cannot represent
It cannot be used together with model.fit()
It removes the need for specifying an Input layer entirely
explanation: Unlike Sequential, which only supports a straight chain of layers, the Functional API lets you wire layers together into any acyclic graph structure, including branches that merge back together, multiple inputs/outputs, and layers reused across different parts of the graph.

q: What is the purpose of overriding train_step() in a custom tf.keras.Model subclass?
options: To completely replace model.fit() with a totally separate custom loop the user must call manually

To customize exactly what happens during a single training step (e.g., custom loss handling, multiple optimizers, adversarial updates) while still being able to use the convenience of model.fit(), including its callbacks, progress bar, and distribution-strategy support
To disable backpropagation for that model entirely
To force the model to always use SGD as its optimizer
explanation: Overriding train_step() lets you inject custom logic into what happens for one batch (like GAN-style alternating updates) while still benefiting from fit()'s built-in orchestration — callbacks, metrics tracking, distributed training support — rather than writing an entirely separate training loop.

q: What must a custom train_step() implementation typically return?
options: The updated model weights as a raw Python list
A dictionary mapping metric names to their current values, which is the format fit()'s progress bar and returned History object expect
Nothing; return values from train_step() are always ignored
The full computation graph as a serialized protobuf
explanation: fit() expects train_step() to return a dict of metric_name -> value (typically including the loss and any tracked metrics) so it can update the progress bar during training and populate the History object it ultimately returns.

q: Within a custom train_step(), what is the purpose of using self.compiled_loss and self.compiled_metrics?
options: They have no functional purpose and exist only for backward compatibility

They let you conveniently apply the loss function(s) and metrics that were passed to model.compile(), inside your custom train_step, instead of manually reimplementing that loss/metric-tracking logic from scratch
They force the model to ignore whatever loss was specified in model.compile()
They can only be used outside of any custom train_step
explanation: self.compiled_loss and self.compiled_metrics wrap up the loss function(s) and metric objects configured via compile(), so a custom train_step can call them directly to compute the configured loss/metrics rather than duplicating that logic manually.

q: In the Keras Functional API, what does reusing the exact same Dense layer instance across two different input branches accomplish?
options: It creates two entirely independent copies of that layer with separate weights
It ties (shares) the weights between both branches, since the same underlying layer object — and therefore the same trainable weights — is applied to both inputs
It automatically deletes one of the two branches
It disables training for that particular layer
explanation: Calling the same layer object on two different symbolic inputs in the Functional API reuses that layer's single set of weights for both calls, meaning any update to those weights affects both branches identically, which is exactly what 'shared layers' means.

q: What is the purpose of the loss_weights argument to model.compile() when a model has multiple named outputs, each with its own loss?
options: It sets the batch size used for each individual output
It scales the relative contribution of each output's individual loss when they are summed together into the single total loss used for backpropagation
It disables gradient computation for all but one output
It changes which optimizer is used for each output
explanation: When a multi-output model has a separate loss per output, loss_weights lets you control how much each output's loss contributes to the overall combined loss that gradients are computed from, e.g., prioritizing one task's objective more heavily than another's.

q: What is the purpose of tf.keras.Model.add_loss()?
options: To register a totally separate, unrelated Keras model for later use

To add an arbitrary additional loss term (e.g., an activity regularization term depending on a layer's inputs/outputs) that is automatically included in the model's total loss during training, outside of the standard y_true-vs-y_pred loss functions
To permanently disable the loss configured via model.compile()
To change a model's input shape at runtime
explanation: add_loss() lets a layer or model contribute extra loss terms computed from arbitrary internal quantities (not necessarily tied to labeled targets), and Keras automatically adds these into the total loss used for gradient computation during training.

q: What is the purpose of tf.keras.Model.add_metric() called inside a layer or model's call()?
options: To permanently replace the optimizer

To log a custom metric derived from intermediate values available inside call() (e.g., statistics of an internal activation), without needing to route that value through the standard loss/metrics arguments passed to compile()
To disable metric tracking for the rest of training
To force the model to stop training immediately
explanation: add_metric() lets you track arbitrary custom quantities computed during the forward pass (not necessarily comparing predictions to labels) as trackable, loggable metrics, which is useful for monitoring internal model behavior beyond standard prediction-based metrics.

q: Why does model.summary() on a freshly-instantiated subclassed tf.keras.Model often fail to show full layer output shapes until after the model has processed at least one input?
options: Subclassed models can never display a summary under any circumstances

A subclassed model's layers typically infer their shapes lazily from the first actual input passed through call() (or an explicit build() call), unlike Sequential/Functional models, which are constructed with known Input shapes from the start
summary() is exclusively a debugging tool unrelated to shapes
It's a bug present in every version of TensorFlow with no workaround
explanation: Because a subclassed model's forward computation is defined imperatively in call() rather than declared upfront via explicit Input tensors, layer shapes often aren't known until the model actually runs on real data (or build() is called explicitly with an input shape), unlike the Functional/Sequential APIs.

q: What is the key practical difference between calling model(x) directly versus model.predict(x)?
options: They are strictly identical in every situation with no differences at all

model(x) runs the model as a direct callable (useful, e.g., inside a custom training step under a GradientTape), while model.predict() handles batching internally, runs in inference mode, and is optimized for large-scale, memory-efficient batch inference
model.predict() cannot be used on data larger than a single batch
model(x) always returns a Python list instead of a tensor
explanation: model(x) is the more 'raw' functional call typically used inside custom computation (e.g., training steps needing gradients), whereas model.predict() is a higher-level convenience method that manages batching and memory for potentially very large inputs, defaulting to inference-mode behavior.

q: What is the effect of setting model.trainable = False on an entire Keras model used as a submodel within a larger model?
options: It has no effect unless applied to every individual layer separately with identical syntax

It freezes all the weights of that entire submodel as a block (commonly used in transfer learning to treat a pretrained model as a fixed feature extractor), and this freezing must be set before the outer model is compiled to actually take effect
It permanently deletes all of that submodel's weights
It converts the submodel into a non-differentiable lookup table
explanation: Setting trainable = False on a whole model marks all of its weights as non-trainable at once — a common transfer-learning pattern — but for this to actually change which weights the optimizer updates, the containing model generally needs to be (re)compiled after making this change.

q: Why might a frozen (trainable=False) submodel containing BatchNorm layers still need to be explicitly called with training=False to be fully 'frozen' in the way usually intended?
options: training=False has no relationship to BatchNorm behavior at all

Setting trainable=False stops BatchNorm's gamma/beta from being updated by the optimizer, but by default the layer may still compute and use the current batch's statistics during the forward pass unless explicitly run in inference mode, where it instead uses its fixed running statistics
BatchNorm layers are automatically deleted whenever trainable is set to False
training=False permanently disables the entire submodel from ever running again
explanation: trainable=False only affects whether an optimizer updates a layer's weights; BatchNorm's forward-pass behavior (batch statistics vs. stored running statistics) is separately controlled by the training argument, so both need to be handled for full 'freeze' behavior often intended in transfer learning.

q: What is the purpose of implementing get_config() (and typically from_config()) on a custom Keras layer or model subclass?
options: To increase the model's training speed

To enable proper serialization: get_config() returns a dictionary describing the object's configuration so it (or a clone) can later be reconstructed, which tools like model saving/loading or clone_model rely on
To permanently disable saving that layer to disk
To automatically generate unit tests for the layer
explanation: Custom layers/models need to describe their own configuration via get_config() (and typically a matching from_config()) so that saving/loading mechanisms and utilities like clone_model() know how to faithfully recreate an equivalent instance later.

q: What is the purpose of the tf.keras.utils.register_keras_serializable decorator applied to a custom loss, metric, or layer class?
options: It permanently converts the class into a built-in Keras class

It registers the custom class under a name/package so Keras's serialization machinery can automatically look it up by name when loading a saved model, avoiding the need to always manually pass a custom_objects dictionary
It disables the ability to save models containing that class
It forces the class to always run in eager mode
explanation: Registering a custom class lets Keras's save/load machinery resolve it by its registered name automatically, so a saved model or config referencing that custom class can typically be reloaded directly, without having to manually supply custom_objects every time.

q: How does the static graph information available for a Functional API model compare to that of a subclassed model, for tools like plot_model() or model.summary() before any data has been passed through?
options: Both approaches provide identical, complete static graph information immediately upon construction

A Functional model's layer connectivity graph is known at construction time (from the explicit Input tensors and layer calls used to build it), so tools like plot_model() and a full summary() work immediately; a subclassed model's forward logic lives imperatively inside call(), so that static graph view generally isn't directly available without extra steps
Subclassed models always provide richer static graph visualization than Functional models
Neither API ever supports model.summary() under any configuration
explanation: Because the Functional API builds the model by explicitly wiring symbolic Input tensors through layers, the resulting DAG of connections is known immediately and can be visualized/summarized right away, whereas a subclassed model's actual computation graph is only implicitly defined by running call(), limiting upfront static introspection.

q: What does tf.keras.callbacks.LearningRateScheduler let you do that differs from ReduceLROnPlateau?
options: It can only ever keep the learning rate perfectly constant

It lets you set the learning rate as an arbitrary, predetermined function of the epoch index (and optionally the current learning rate), applied proactively at the start of each epoch, rather than reactively waiting for a monitored metric to plateau
It disables the use of any optimizer
It requires no function to be specified at all
explanation: LearningRateScheduler applies a user-supplied schedule function (based purely on epoch number) at the beginning of every epoch, giving you full proactive control over the LR trajectory, unlike ReduceLROnPlateau, which reacts only after detecting stagnation in a monitored metric.

q: How does using a tf.keras.optimizers.schedules.LearningRateSchedule object (like ExponentialDecay) passed directly to an optimizer differ from using an epoch-level LearningRateScheduler callback?
options: They are functionally identical with no meaningful difference

A schedule object is baked directly into the optimizer and updates the learning rate on every individual optimizer step based on the internal iteration counter (and its state is properly saved/restored with optimizer checkpoints), whereas a callback typically only adjusts the learning rate at epoch boundaries via Python
Schedule objects can only be used with the SGD optimizer
Callbacks update the learning rate more frequently than any schedule object ever could
explanation: A LearningRateSchedule is evaluated as a function of the optimizer's own step counter on every single update, integrates properly with optimizer state checkpointing, and can vary within an epoch, whereas a callback-based approach generally only changes the rate once per epoch from the Python side.

q: What is the purpose of the tf.keras.callbacks.CSVLogger callback?
options: It permanently deletes training logs after each epoch
It streams per-epoch metric values to a CSV file on disk, providing simple logging for later analysis outside of tools like TensorBoard

q: What does the tf.keras.callbacks.TerminateOnNaN callback do?

It only checks for NaN values once, at the very end of training
explanation: TerminateOnNaN monitors the loss after each batch and halts training right away if it encounters a NaN or infinite value, avoiding continued compute on a training run that has already numerically diverged.

q: What role does the (usually implicit, default) progress-bar logging component play during a typical model.fit() call?
options: It permanently prevents any other callback from running
It renders the console progress bar showing per-batch/per-epoch progress and current metric values as training proceeds, and is included by default unless verbose output is explicitly turned off
It only displays information after training has fully completed
It replaces the need for specifying any loss function

q: What is the purpose of TensorBoard's Profiler plugin, beyond the basic scalar/histogram logging the TensorBoard callback provides?
options: It only shows the final test-set accuracy as a single number

It captures detailed per-operation and per-device timing traces, helping diagnose performance bottlenecks such as whether training is input-pipeline-bound, communication-bound, or bottlenecked by a specific slow op, beyond simple metric curves
It automatically retrains the model with better hyperparameters
It disables GPU usage while profiling
explanation: The Profiler plugin provides fine-grained execution traces (op-level timing, device utilization, input pipeline analysis) that go well beyond the scalar/histogram summaries the standard TensorBoard callback logs, which is essential for diagnosing why training is slow.

q: In a custom training loop (not using model.fit()), what is the purpose of calling tf.summary.scalar() within a tf.summary.create_file_writer() context?
options: It permanently changes the model's loss function

It manually logs a scalar value (such as the current loss) to an event file so it can be visualized later in TensorBoard, replicating what the built-in TensorBoard callback would otherwise automatically handle inside model.fit()
It disables eager execution for the rest of the program
It forces the optimizer to use a fixed learning rate
explanation: Since a custom training loop doesn't get the automatic logging that the Keras TensorBoard callback provides during fit(), tf.summary.scalar() calls within an active file-writer context let you manually write out chosen values (like loss per step) for later inspection in TensorBoard.

q: What does setting write_graph=True in the Keras TensorBoard callback accomplish?
options: It logs the model's computation graph structure to TensorBoard's 'Graphs' tab for visualization, useful for verifying architecture, at the cost of extra logging overhead/storage
It permanently disables writing any scalar metrics
It forces the model to retrain from a blank graph every epoch
It converts the model into a fully connected network regardless of its original architecture
explanation: write_graph=True tells the callback to also serialize and log the model's underlying computation graph so it can be explored visually in TensorBoard's Graphs tab, which is useful for sanity-checking architecture but adds to the size/overhead of the generated logs.

q: What does the embeddings_freq parameter of the Keras TensorBoard callback control?
